newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Western chocolate firms eye sweet future in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Western chocolate firms eye sweet future in Russia.

text.p: Western confectioners are looking East to tap the potentially huge Russian chocolate market by setting up plants on Russian soil as well as boosting imports, company officials said on Friday.

British confectionery giant Cadbury Schweppes Plc officially opened a 40,000-tonne chocolate factory in Russia's northwest on Friday, just five days after Germany's Stollwerck AG opened a 20,000-tonne plant near Moscow.

"We would expect to see a combination of a rise in market share in Russia and, through the rise in the number of (chocolate) products on offer, ongoing growth in Russian demand," said Dora McCabe, head of public relations for Cadbury.
Cadbury spent $120 million and Stollwerck over 50 million marks ($28 million) on their plants, as sign of their long term commitments.

Both companies said they had built their factories in the European part of Russia to tap the most concentrated areas of demand in Moscow and St Petersburg, where per capita consumption is said to be not far below Western countries.
"We will sell the bulk of our chocolate bars in Moscow, where we already have over a quarter of the market share," a Stollwerck spokeswoman said.
Deeper penetration into the Urals, and further east across Siberia and the Far East would be a far less attractive move, analysts said.
Russia has developed a sweet tooth for Western confectionery goods ever since economic reforms began in 1991.
International chocolate-making giants like Cadbury, Masterfoods of the United States and Nestle of Switzerland moved quickly to fill the gap by exporting ready-made products to post-Communist Russia.
"Initially the growth was dramatic," Cadbury's McCabe said. "From a few hundred tonnes of our products, the market grew to 20,000-odd tonnes in just two to three years."
Cadbury estimates Russia's total sweet market, including sugar and chocolate-based goods, at a million tonnes.
And analysts see the market expanding as Russia emerges from its backward economic past and disposable incomes start to rise.
"I do think Russia is a bullish market in terms of demand," a senior London-based analyst said.

Robert Flemings Securities Ltd pegged Russian chocolate confectionery demand at 511,000 tonnes by 2000, up 34 percent from 381,000 tonnes in 1996. It based its forecasts on estimates by market research company ERC Statistics International.

The London analyst said Western firms like Cadbury, Nestle, Masterfoods and Stollwerck were investing in production within Russia to save money long-term by tapping cheaper labour markets and cutting transport costs.
But Cadbury said the reason was more simple.
"We reached the limit of our capacity at other facilities, and at one stage we were even exporting to Russia from our plants in South Africa and India," McCabe said.
The war for market share is hotting up in Russia, with Red October KROT.RTS, the largest domestic producer, already toppled from number one spot by Masterfoods.

Russian and foreign sweet makers advertise regularly on television, and even President Boris Yeltsin got in on the act in April, urging Russians to eat more home-made chocolate, because he thought it was better than imports.
